title: Python, arrays & vectorized thinking
summary: Learn the programming concepts that connect ordinary code to numerical computing.
html:
Learn the programming concepts that connect ordinary code to numerical computing.

How the pieces connect

Specify shapes → Transform → Validate → Measure. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it.

Names, values, and mutation

A Python name refers to an object. Assignment can create another reference rather than another copy. Lists are flexible containers; numerical arrays store elements with a dtype and shape. Mutating an array view can modify the original storage, so understand whether an operation returns a view or a copy.

Shape is part of the contract

A batch of 32 feature vectors with 128 features has shape (32,128). A weight matrix of shape (128,10) maps it to (32,10). Write dimensions next to each intermediate. Broadcasting expands compatible dimensions conceptually; it may avoid copying inputs but still produce a very large output.

Vectorization and the runtime

Calling an array operation delegates loops to compiled numerical code. This reduces Python interpreter overhead and can use SIMD or GPU kernels. It does not make the computational complexity disappear. A vectorized pairwise distance calculation over a million points may still allocate an impossible trillion-entry result.

Build reproducible experiments

Use isolated environments and record dependency versions. Set seeds when comparing runs, but do not assume identical results across hardware or kernels. Keep preprocessing, model code, data versions, and evaluation settings together. Assertions about shapes and finite values catch errors closer to their source.

Worked example

import numpy as np
x = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
w = np.array([[2.], [-1.]])
y = x @ w
assert y.shape == (2, 1)
print(y.ravel())  # [0. 2.]

What goes wrong

Elementwise multiplication (*) and matrix multiplication (@) answer different questions. A computation can run without a shape error and still broadcast along the wrong axis.

Check your understanding

What is the result shape of (8,16) @ (16,4)?

Reveal the explanation

(8,4). The matching inner dimension is summed over; the outer dimensions remain.

An operating model for python, arrays & vectorized thinking

Numerical programming is a discipline of contracts. A tensor shape is not decoration: it records which examples, positions, features, heads, or channels an operation is acting on. Most subtle errors occur when an operation is legal under broadcasting but semantically applies an axis in the wrong role.

The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test.

Worked system: the broadcast that silently changes the experiment

Suppose a batch of four examples has shape [4, 3]: four rows and three features. You intend to subtract one mean per feature, so the mean must have shape [3] and broadcasts across rows. If you instead compute a mean with shape [4, 1], Python and NumPy will still produce a legal [4, 3] result—but it subtracts one value per example. There is no exception because both operations are mathematically defined. The failure is semantic: the array library cannot know whether your first axis means examples, time, heads, or channels.

Use a tiny matrix whose expected result can be calculated by hand. Print every shape at an operation boundary, assert finiteness after divisions or exponentials, and name axes in comments or a typed tensor library. This is not defensive ceremony. In ML code, a silently broadcast loss can improve while training the wrong objective, and a transposed attention tensor can return plausible values with the wrong positions interacting.

Notebook: Trace a byte budget

Keep a tiny hand-calculated input beside every new operation. Print shapes and a few values, then compare the vectorized result to a simple loop before scaling it.

items = 1_000_000
bytes_per_item = 4
working_set = items * bytes_per_item
print(f"{working_set / 2**20:.1f} MiB")
# Now include every copy, index, and temporary buffer.
What to test next. 1. Specify shapes: Name every axis and its semantic meaning. 2. Transform: Use array operations with an explicit dtype. 3. Validate: Assert shape, range, finiteness, and alignment. 4. Measure: Benchmark representative sizes and allocations.

The gotcha. A small inspection script proves only the quantities it prints. Preserve units, shapes, versions, and the input fixture beside its output.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Specify shapes. Name every axis and its semantic meaning.
  2. Transform. Use array operations with an explicit dtype.
  3. Validate. Assert shape, range, finiteness, and alignment.
  4. Measure. Benchmark representative sizes and allocations.

Keep a tiny hand-calculated input beside every new operation. Print shapes and a few values, then compare the vectorized result to a simple loop before scaling it.

Verification questions for python, arrays & vectorized thinking

BoundaryQuestionEvidence
Specify shapesWhat would show that this boundary failed?Name every axis and its semantic meaning.
TransformWhat would show that this boundary failed?Use array operations with an explicit dtype.
ValidateWhat would show that this boundary failed?Assert shape, range, finiteness, and alignment.
MeasureWhat would show that this boundary failed?Benchmark representative sizes and allocations.

The gotcha. Passing each component check separately does not prove the composed path preserves identity, units, ordering, or authority.

Names, identity, and ownership

Assignment binds a name to an object; it does not promise a copy. This matters when configurations, containers, iterators, and numerical views carry mutable state across experiments.

  • Identity differs from equality. is tests shared identity; == compares values.
  • Mutable defaults persist across calls. Create per-call state inside the function.
  • Shallow copies retain nested aliases. Define which layer owns mutation.
  • Generators are consumable state. An exhausted iterator can produce an empty evaluation pass without an exception.

The gotcha. A fixed seed cannot control hidden mutation from an earlier run.

Shape, dtype, strides, and offset define an array

An ndarray is a view over a buffer. Shape gives logical extents; strides give byte steps; dtype determines representation and arithmetic.

  • Reshape may change only metadata. An incompatible layout forces a copy.
  • Transpose usually changes strides. A later kernel may materialize contiguous storage.
  • Basic slicing often returns a view. Advanced indexing commonly returns a copy.
  • Broadcasting aligns axes from the right. It can avoid copying an input while allocating a huge output.

The gotcha. Compatible dimensions do not prove compatible axis meanings.

Vectorization changes the cost model

Array operations move loops into compiled kernels. Fusion avoids intermediates; batching amortizes overhead; reductions introduce ordering and numerical choices.

  • Benchmark synchronization boundaries. Reading an accelerator scalar may wait for queued work.
  • Keep a slow oracle. Verify optimized operations against a transparent implementation on tiny inputs.
  • Test invariants. Assert shape, finiteness, normalization, masking, and expected transformations.

The gotcha. A one-line expression can allocate several arrays and perform quadratic work.
